text: A lot of Christians these days would do
well to remember the prophetic critique.
Hey everybody, I'm Dan Mlelen. I'm a
scholar of the Bible and religion. And
if you're not familiar with the
prophetic critique, it's a rhetorical
pattern that originates in the 8th
century prophets. And we see it popping
up in a few different places all the way
down to the Gospel of Matthew in the New
Testament. And this pattern has the
prophets representing God as hating and
rejecting
the performance of sacrifices and
offerings and festivals that are
required by the law of Moses. So for
instance, we will have one prophet say,
"I do not delight in the blood of bulls
or your new moons and your Sabbaths my
soul hates." Or, "I will have mercy and
not sacrifice." And so you see this in
Isaiah and in Jeremiah and Hosea and
Amos and Micah and Zechariah and
elsewhere. And scholars for a long time
have said, "Oh, these are
protorotestants. They hate ritual. They
really just love faith." And that's not
what's going on at all. To understand
the prophetic critique, you've got to
start with the observation that for all
of these prophets, the purpose of the
law of Moses was the generation and
curation of a just and a righteous
society where everybody has what they
need to get by. And in this system, the
canaries in the coal mine of cosmic and
social justice and order were the orphan
and the widow and the poor and the
oppressed and the foreigner. So if they
were doing bad, that portended bad
things for the rest of society. And so
what the prophets are pointing out is
that the wealthy and the elite and the
privileged and the powerful were
exploiting the law to benefit themselves
while behind everybody's back grinding
the faces of the poor and taking
advantage of the economy and the ritual
system and the justice system to hurt
the canaries in the coal mine of cosmic
and social justice and order while
performing outwardly the displays of
piety so that they could advance their
own interests within this society. And
so what the prophets are representing
God as hating is the leveraging of the
performance of these sacrifices and
offerings and festivals to advance one's
own interests on the backs of the widow
and the orphan and the poor and the
oppressed and the foreigner. And so when
Jesus says, "Go and learn what that
means. I will have mercy and not
sacrifice. He's talking to the people
that he calls hypocrites for praying on
the street corner to be seen of men. He
says they have their reward because
they're doing this not to advance
society or their own relationship with
God. They're doing it in order to
advance their own interests within the
society over and against the express
purposes of the law. That's what the
prophetic critique is and that's what a
lot of Christians today are ignoring as
they try to champion the advance of
Christianity within society. And the fit
for this video is Spider-Man.
